name: Chin strap while sleeping

lead: A chin strap is a band that holds the mouth closed during sleep. Followers use it to encourage nasal breathing and a closed-mouth resting posture, often alongside mewing or mouth taping, with the hope of better jaw development.

It works mechanically by stopping the jaw dropping open while asleep. Reference sources note that chronic mouth breathing in children is associated with dental and facial changes such as a long, narrow face. No published trial located has tested chin straps for appearance.

paras: It is worn nightly as part of a routine with mewing, tongue posture work or mouth taping. Users generally describe it as a long-term habit rather than a quick change.
Mouth breathing usually reflects nasal congestion, and reference sources advise treating the cause. The health effects of related mouth taping are described as little researched.

web.title: Mouth taping systematic review - PLoS One 2025

angle.text: A closed-mouth, nasal-breathing posture that followers hope supports a better jaw and face. A strap keeps the mouth shut overnight. The link to facial reshaping is based on user reports; no trial has tested it for appearance.

lead: A chin strap worn during sleep is a band that wraps under the jaw and over the head to keep the mouth closed overnight. In looksmaxxing communities it is used to encourage nasal breathing and a closed-mouth resting posture, with the aim of supporting a stronger jawline and better facial posture, and it is often paired with mewing or mouth taping.[1][2]

The reasoning follows from what is known about breathing and face shape in children. Chronic mouth breathing in childhood is associated with dental and facial changes such as a long, narrow face and open bite, and treatment is described as addressing nasal congestion and building nasal breathing habits.[1] Proponents extend this to adults, saying a closed mouth and nasal breathing during sleep keeps the tongue and jaw in what they consider a better position. Reference sources note that the health effects of mouth taping, a related practice, have been little researched.[1]

In medicine, chin straps have been used mainly alongside CPAP machines to reduce mouth leak and in snoring and sleep apnoea studies. A 2025 systematic review of mouth taping and related methods included two studies that used chin straps.[3]
infobox: Adjunct to CPAP to reduce mouth leak[3]

paras: The strap wraps under the jaw and over the head to keep the lower jaw from dropping open. Believers say this trains nasal breathing and jaw posture. Chin straps of this kind are also sold for snoring and are used in sleep clinics with CPAP masks.[3]

Chronic mouth breathing in children may affect dental and facial growth and can lead to a long, narrow face, anterior open bite and tongue-thrusting habits.[1] In about 85 percent of cases mouth breathing is an adaptation to nasal congestion, often during sleep, and descriptions recommend treating the underlying cause and building a habit of nasal breathing.[1] Less common causes include polyps and a short upper lip that does not close at rest.[1]

A 2025 systematic review in PLoS One examined mouth taping in people with mouth breathing, sleep-disordered breathing or obstructive sleep apnoea. It covered ten studies, two of which used chin straps, and concluded that mouth taping is not supported as a clinical intervention and that benefits appear limited outside mild sleep apnoea.[3]

Of the two chin strap studies, one found the strap reduced mouth leak during nasal CPAP and lowered snoring, without significantly changing oxygen desaturation; the other found no significant change in apnoea-hypopnoea index or oxygen nadir.[3] The review lists risks of taping when the nose is blocked, including asphyxiation and aspiration.[3]

Mewing, a related oral-posture practice, is described as unproven; the American Association of Orthodontists says there is no evidence it improves the jaw.[2] Snoring treatments described in general references include lifestyle changes, nasal dilators, dental appliances that move the lower jaw forward, myofunctional exercises and CPAP.[4] In obstructive sleep apnoea, positional and dental-appliance approaches are described.[5]

No studies found of chin straps for facial appearance. Studies of chin straps in sleep medicine are small: a 2003 study found a chin strap reduced mouth leak during nasal CPAP and lowered snoring, and a 2015 study found no significant change in apnoea-hypopnoea index, both reported in a 2025 systematic review.[3]

timeline.event: Study reports a chin strap reduced mouth leak and snoring during nasal CPAP.[3]
Study of chin strap use in sleep apnoea finds no significant change in apnoea-hypopnoea index.[3]
Systematic review in PLoS One assesses mouth taping and chin straps.[3]
